reason: 'Same technology is a control on one side and a weapon on the other' only fits one item: ransomware, where encryption is the weapon. It tells the learner to move that item out of Confidentiality without explaining why. The 'property, not technology' part teaches a method, but the second sentence points at one specific item. It does not choose between Integrity and Availability, so MED rather than HIGH.

'Sees / changes / can't use' is just the definition of C/I/A, which any correct method has to use. 'Even if other damage follows' quietly settles the ransomware question (it modifies data, but the goal is denial of use) and the exfiltrate-and-post question (it can look like an integrity or reputation harm). Those are real ambiguity calls, but the learner still has to judge what the attacker's goal was. The leak is borderline but still LOW.

factual_problem: 'Two of these properties involve identity' implies Privacy doesn't, yet privacy is about personally identifiable information. That's loose wording. Also, a tamper-evident audit log gives accountability more than strict non-repudiation, which needs the action bound cryptographically to the actor. The hint frames non-repudiation as 'evidence someone else could check later', which pulls the log item into that bucket on a weak footing.
reason: This is the defining distinction, but it collapses into a before/after timing shortcut. Items that say 'Requiring...' or 'Unlocking...' go to 'before they act', and items that say 'log of who changed' or 'signing...so it traces' go to 'evidence...later'. Wording alone sorts all four identity items without knowing what non-repudiation guarantees.

'The individual's control over information about themselves' repeats the erase item ('what you hold about them') almost word for word, so that item matches by surface text. Data minimisation still needs some thought. 'Who is acting and what they did' also restates both identity buckets.

Machine / rule people follow / physical barrier is the definition of the three types. The learner still has to see that a background check is a process and that full-disk encryption is technical even though it protects a physical laptop. Fence and door are trivially physical either way.

factual_problem: The 'everyone stops following instructions' test is unreliable. A locked door also depends on people locking it and not propping it open, and the test only separates administrative from everything else, not technical from physical. A learner who applies it literally may treat the server-room door as people-dependent.
reason: 'Paperwork or not' is aimed at one item: background checks, the only administrative item with no document attached. That steers it into Administrative and away from Technical or Physical, which goes beyond teaching a method.

'Would you owe this even if nobody had hired you' gets matched against the item text. The mentoring item says 'no billable work attached' and the sales-pitch item involves a 'prospect' (not hired), so both are pushed out of III with no thought. The follow-up words then work as keywords: 'harm reaching the public' matches patients and city dispatch (I), and 'the field as a whole' matches mentoring and exam-leak reporting (IV). Together that narrows about five of the eight items by surface wording.

factual_problem: Misleading. 'Honesty won't separate the canons on its own' discourages the learner from using honesty as the signal. But the prompt itself defines Canon II as 'your own honesty and legality', and the sales-pitch item (declining to exaggerate a threat, i.e. avoiding unnecessary alarm) belongs under Canon II precisely because it is about honesty. The hint fights the prompt and pushes that item toward III or I.
reason: 'An engagement you have taken on' matches the conflict-of-interest item, which contains the word 'current engagement', so it lands in III by string match. The rest restates the four canon subjects already given in the prompt.
Dependency-chain reasoning is a pure method. It names no step and pins no position.

'Deciding, doing and signing off' lines up word for word with three items: 'Choose a treatment' = deciding, 'Apply the control' = doing, 'formally accepted' = signing off. The second sentence then fixes sign-off after apply/verify. That gives the order of steps 3, 4 and 5 by keyword matching, with no understanding of residual risk needed. Identify-then-assess is obvious enough that the whole sequence falls out.

The method is definitional, but each clause works as a surface decoder. 'Only advised' matches 'Where practical, prefer' (Guideline). 'Series of actions' matches 'Step 1...' and 'click Report, then forward' (Procedure). 'Named technology or setting' matches AES-256 (Standard). 'From inside the organisation' matches HIPAA (Law). The worst is the word 'responsibility' in 'goal or responsibility with no how': it is tailored to the 'named owner who is accountable' item, which is the main must-but-not-a-standard trap, and it hands that item to Policy.

Both sentences each disarm one specific distractor. 'Can bind everyone and still name no product, setting or step' targets 'Every system must have a named owner' (Policy, not Standard). 'Naming exactly what to use is not telling you how' targets 'must run the approved hardened OS image' and AES-256 (Standard, not Procedure). These are pre-solved trap items, not a general method.
